title: Paul McCartney pleads guilty to cannabis cultivation | 1973
content:
On 8 March 1973 Paul McCartney pleaded guilty to cannabis cultivation at Campbeltown Sheriff Court, Scotland.

It followed a police raid at his Scottish properties on 19 September 1972, in which eight officers found a total of five cannabis plants. McCartney was charged three days later on two counts of possession and one of cultivating cannabis. A not guilty plea was submitted in absentia to all three charges, and a trial was set for this date.

Paul and Linda McCartney and Linda arrived in Scotland by private jet, hired for £1,000. Their solicitor Len Murray had enlisted barrister barrister John McCluskey to represent Paul at the hearing.

Prior to the trial, McCluskey noticed some procedural errors in two of the charges, noting that the plants were not mature enough to produce cannabis resin. A meeting was called with the prosecutor, Iain Stewart, during which it was agreed that the two charges of possession would be dropped if the one of cultivation was accepted. McCartney was told the news an hour before the hearing began, and agreed to accept the charge.

In court McCluskey argued that McCartney had been sent the seeds by fans, and had planted them without knowing what they were. No effort had been made to conceal the plants, he noted. He added that a conviction could be potentially disastrous for future international tours.

Sheriff Donald McDiarmid summed up by first suggesting a punitive reaction would be in order. “I take into account that the seeds were sent to you as a gift,” he said when summing up, “but I also take into account that you are a public figure of considerable interest to young people and I must deal with you accordingly.”

A charge of £100 was levied, which the multi-millionaire McCartney was given 14 days to pay – a decision which was greeted with laughter in the courtroom. He and Linda later flew back to London in their private jet.

McCluskey later noted that, although Paul appeared to take the trial seriously, Linda appeared “stoned out of her mind” and insisted on wearing McCluskey’s bowler hat throughout the proceedings.

Outside, a relaxed and unrepentant McCartney joked with reporters, describing the sheriff as “a great guy” and saying he believed cannabis to be less harmful than alcohol. Linda giggled at her husband’s side, apparently still stoned.
